research_method.claude: Convergent mixed-methods design: project telemetry (Jira, GitHub/GitLab, SonarQube) analysed with descriptives, Pearson correlations, hierarchical multiple regression, separate regressions per DORA metric, compound interest model calibrated by nonlinear least squares, cost-benefit analysis (ROI, break-even); 47-item structured survey (descriptives, t-test; CFA/SEM announced but not reported)
research_method.nlm: Convergent mixed-methods design combining quantitative panel data (DevOps toolchain telemetry) and a survey; regression models for velocity and defect density, calibrated compound interest model, ROI and cost-of-delay calculations
research_method.value: Convergent mixed-methods design; quantitative project-level telemetry from Jira, GitHub/GitLab and SonarQube analysed with descriptive statistics, correlations, hierarchical multiple regression (delivery velocity, defect density) and regressions on the four DORA metrics; compound interest debt model calibrated by nonlinear least squares (52 projects); cost-benefit analysis of remediation (ROI, break-even; 34 projects); structured 47-item Likert survey of software engineering leaders
research_method.note: Statistical details (nonlinear least squares, 47 items, subsets of 52 and 34 projects) given only by Claude, not contradicted by NotebookLM.

context.claude: Industry; 89 enterprise projects from 23 unnamed organizations (financial services 27, healthcare technology 19, enterprise SaaS 24, telecommunications 19); survey of 412 software engineering leaders; abstract places survey in North American enterprises, methods give no project geography
context.nlm: Enterprise software systems; 89 projects across 23 organizations (financial services 27, healthcare technology 19, enterprise SaaS 24, telecommunications 19) in North America; 412 software engineering leaders surveyed
context.value: industry; 89 enterprise software projects from 23 organizations (financial services n = 27, healthcare technology n = 19, enterprise SaaS n = 24, telecommunications n = 19); survey of 412 software engineering leaders (North American enterprises per abstract)
context.note: NotebookLM places the projects in North America; Claude says only the abstract gives geography (for the survey), so geography is attached to the survey only.

dora_applied.note: The four DORA metrics are operationalized from telemetry and used as dependent variables.

space_applied.note: Claude: SPACE claimed in abstract/validity section but no variable mapped to a SPACE dimension (referenced only); NotebookLM: applied to conceptualize multidimensional productivity.

ai_discussed.note: Claude: AI-generated code only named as an unaddressed limitation/future work; NotebookLM: examines impact of AI-generated code/LLMs on technical debt. Full text shows only intro and limitation mentions.

remote_covid.note: Work mode not reported by either.

data_window.note: Not stated by either (only mean project duration of 34.2 months in Claude).

cat_productivity.note: Delivery velocity (story points per sprint normalized by team size).

cat_quality.note: Defect density, test coverage, cyclomatic complexity, duplication, change failure rate, MTTR, technical debt ratio.

cat_collaboration.note: No collaboration metric; code review only in recommendations.

cat_satisfaction.note: NotebookLM lists job satisfaction/intent to leave (Besker et al.) as a metric; Claude reports no satisfaction measure. Full text cites Besker et al. only in the literature review.

cat_activity.note: Borderline: commit frequency, PR cycle time, merge conflict frequency and code churn extracted from GitHub, but Claude notes they do not appear in reported results.

cat_delivery.note: Deployment frequency and lead time for changes.

cat_devex.note: NotebookLM tags job satisfaction 'DevEx / Satisfaction', but the DevEx framework is not used.

cat_agile.note: Borderline: projects are agile and velocity is per sprint (counted under productivity); 15-20% sprint-capacity allocation is a recommendation, not a metric.

cat_survey.note: 47-item Likert survey of 412 engineering leaders, including perceived impact on DORA metrics.

evidence.quote: This study employs a convergent mixed-methods design (Creswell & Creswell, 2018) integrating quantitative analysis of project-level telemetry data with structured survey data from software engineering leaders.
The debt growth trajectory was fitted to the compound interest function TDcost (t) = TDprincipal · (1 + r)t using nonlinear least squares estimation.

The quantitative dataset comprises panel data from 89 enterprise software projects across 23 organizations in the financial services (n = 27), healthcare technology (n = 19), enterprise SaaS (n = 24), and telecommunications (n = 19) sectors.
with survey data from 412 software engineering leaders across North American enterprises

DORA metrics were operationalized as follows. Deployment frequency was measured as the number of production deployments per month. Lead time for changes was measured as the median elapsed time from code commit to production deployment, in hours.
